meta.blurb: At nineteen, Nell and Sam sit on a wooden jetty and promise to meet there every July. Then come other people, a ship at sea and a summer when only one of them turns up. How long can a promise last?
meta.bible: Nell Hartley: a piano tuner from Linden Quay, nineteen in the first July and about twenty-seven at the end, practical, funny and slow to say what she feels. Sam Adeyemi: a boatbuilder's son who trains as a ship's engineer, warm, restless and loyal. Linden Quay: the small town on Lake Verna. Lake Verna: the lake. Lantern Night: the town festival on the second Saturday of July, when paper lanterns with wishes are floated on the lake. Green Jetty: the old wooden jetty where they promise to meet every July at dusk. Brass bolt: Sam's gift, from the first engine he repaired, worn on a string by Nell. Mr Brandt: the old piano tuner who taught Nell and leaves her his tools and his shop on Harbour Lane. Pip: Nell's younger sister, who stays in Linden Quay. Dominic Reyes: a kind dentist in the city, Nell's partner for about two years. Corinne: a ship's navigator, Sam's girlfriend for a time. Marlowe & Sons: the city piano makers. Marlowe Concert Hall: the concert hall where Nell later works. Mr Marlowe: the head of the firm. Rotterdam: where Sam trains. Asia: where Sam's long voyage goes. Joseph Adeyemi: Sam's father, the boatbuilder, who falls ill in the seventh July. Hartley Piano Tuning: the name on the new shop sign. Lantern: the name of the little rowing boat Sam builds. Voice and tone: warm, funny and wistful, a slow love story told one July at a time, with a happy ending.

B1B2: On the second Saturday of July, the town of Linden Quay hangs paper lanterns all along Lake Verna. Nell Hartley, who is nineteen and works with pianos, has come with her heavy tool bag.
The piano in the festival hall has not been tuned for years, and every note sounds wrong. Nell opens it up and works while people watch, and then she plays a short tune to test it.
A tall young man stops in the doorway and listens as the tune rings out. His name is Sam Adeyemi, and his family builds boats at the far end of the lake.
Sam says he will leave for Rotterdam in September to train as a ship's engineer. Nell tells him that she, too, is about to leave, because a piano firm in the city has offered her a job.
Each of them writes a secret wish on a lantern and carries it to the water's edge. The two small lights float out together and slowly move away across the dark lake.
As the lanterns drift far out on the lake, Sam suggests a promise, and they shake hands on it. Wherever they are, and whatever happens, they will meet on the Green Jetty every July at dusk.
They stay up talking until the sky turns pale, and then it is time to go. Nell climbs onto the first bus of the morning and watches Sam wave until the road bends.
In the city, Nell works long days at Marlowe & Sons, the piano makers, and she learns something new every week. Sam sends her letters from Rotterdam, full of small drawings of engines and ships.
A year later, Nell takes the train home for Lantern Night, her heart full of nerves. Sam is already waiting at the Green Jetty, tanned from the sun and grinning from ear to ear.
Late that night Sam borrows his father's rowing boat and takes Nell out onto the water. Halfway across, he laughs so hard that the boat tips over, and they both end up swimming.
Wrapped in blankets on the jetty, Nell nearly tells Sam how she feels. But he starts talking about his first job on a ship, and she cannot find the right moment.
At the station Sam takes a small brass bolt from his pocket. It has a piece of string through it, and he tells her it is for luck.
In her third year at Marlowe & Sons, Nell is chosen to look after the pianos at the Marlowe Concert Hall. There she meets Dominic Reyes, a friendly dentist who loves music but plays very badly.
On the third Lantern Night, Nell is at the Green Jetty before sunset. The lanterns are lit and the music starts, but there is no sign of Sam.
Just before midnight, Sam appears out of the dark, covered in dust and gasping for air. His ship was delayed in port, he explains, and he has run the last three miles from the station.
They sit side by side on the jetty and watch the last lanterns burn out. Neither of them says very much, yet it feels as if something important is waiting to be said.
In spring, Sam writes that he has met a woman called Corinne, who is a navigator on his ship. Nell reads the letter three times and tells herself that she is happy for him.
On the fourth Lantern Night, Sam walks onto the Green Jetty with Corinne beside him. Nell puts on her brightest smile and shakes the stranger's hand.
Corinne is warm, funny and kind, and Nell cannot find a single reason to dislike her. She makes an excuse about an early train and leaves before the lanterns are lit.
On the long night bus, Nell holds the little brass bolt and thinks hard. By the time she reaches the city, she has decided to accept Dominic's invitation to dinner.
For a whole year, Nell and Dominic go to concerts, cook together and walk by the river. He is gentle and dependable, and he never asks her to be anyone but herself.
Dominic is busy at his clinic, so Nell goes to the fifth Lantern Night alone. Sam is there as well, and he tells her quietly that he and Corinne have gone separate ways.
Sam tells her that he has taken a job on a ship that will sail to Asia and back. It will take a year, so he does not know if he can come next July.
That winter, old Mr Brandt dies, the kind tuner who first taught Nell about pianos. In his will he leaves her all his tools and his little shop in Linden Quay.
Nell does not open the shop, even though it belongs to her now. Her job, her friends and Dominic are all in the city, and she is afraid to give up a safe life for a dream.
On the sixth Lantern Night, Nell goes to the jetty anyway, though she knows that Sam is far away at sea. She sits alone until the last lantern has burned out.
Three weeks later, a postcard arrives with a foreign stamp and a picture of a harbour. Sam writes that on Lantern Night he stood on the deck and thought of her.
In the autumn, Dominic takes Nell to their favourite restaurant and asks her to marry him. He is smiling and nervous, and the ring in its small box shines in the candlelight.
Nell tells Dominic that she needs a few weeks to think, and he says that he understands. She walks for hours through the city, asking herself what she really wants.
Nell tells Dominic the truth, and her eyes fill with tears. He holds her hand and says that he has always known part of her was listening for a different piano.
In July, Nell goes to the Green Jetty feeling light and free. She has brought two lanterns, but Sam does not come, and the hours pass.
Before she leaves, Nell writes two words on a piece of paper and folds it small. She hides it under a loose stone beside the bench, where only Sam would think to look.
On the train home, Nell decides that the promise was only a game for two young people. She feels foolish for believing in it for so long.
When July comes again, Nell stays in the city and works on the pianos for a huge summer festival. She tells everyone that she does not mind, and she almost believes it.
Sam has come home for good, because his father fell ill last July and the boatyard needed him. On the jetty he finds a faded note under a loose stone, and it says, I came.
The next morning Sam meets Nell's sister Pip in the market. She is cross with him at first, but then she tells him that Nell works at the Marlowe Concert Hall.
Sam writes Nell a long letter that night, but every sentence sounds wrong. He tears it up and checks the train times instead, because he wants to say it to her face.
In September, Sam takes the train to the city and walks into the Marlowe Concert Hall. On the stage, a woman is bent over a grand piano, and he knows her at once.
Nell sees him and drops her tuning hammer with a loud crash. They walk beside the river for hours while he explains about his father and she tells him about the note.
On a stone bridge, Sam says that he has loved her since the very first Lantern Night. He adds that Corinne knew it, and that was why she left.
Nell tells him that she loves him too, but that she is afraid of losing him again. Sam answers that he is a patient man and will wait as long as she needs.
At midwinter, Nell takes the train to Linden Quay and unlocks the shop on Harbour Lane. The dust is thick and the air is cold, but she feels completely at home.
Back in the city, Nell hands her notice to Mr Marlowe. He is sorry to lose her, but he shakes her hand and wishes her all the best.
In the spring, Sam arrives with his father's van and carries Nell's boxes into the shop. Her sister Pip stands on the pavement and cheers as if she were at a football match.
Sam paints a beautiful sign for the front of the shop, and it says Hartley Piano Tuning in gold letters. On the first morning Nell stands beneath it with a cup of tea and cannot stop smiling.
As the weeks pass, Nell and Sam meet almost every day, for breakfast, for walks, for tea. Sam also begins to build a small boat in the evenings, and he will not tell her who it is for.
On the second Saturday of July, Nell is asked to tune the piano in the festival hall once more. When she has finished, she plays the little tune she played on the very first night.
Sam appears in the doorway, just as he did years before, and hums along with the tune. Nell stops playing and laughs, and they walk down to the Green Jetty together.
At the end of the jetty, a small new boat is tied to the post, and Sam has painted a name on the side. It says Lantern, and he tells Nell that he built it for the two of them.
They each write a wish and show it to the other, and the two wishes are exactly the same. Then they kiss on the Green Jetty while the lanterns float out across the lake together.
C1C2: Every July, on the second Saturday, the little town of Linden Quay lights hundreds of paper lanterns and sets them glowing along the shore of Lake Verna. Nell Hartley, nineteen years old and still half an apprentice, pushed her way through the crowd with a heavy bag of tuning tools on her shoulder. She had been sent on an errand by her old teacher, and she was already late.

The old upright in the festival hall had stood untouched through a damp winter, and its notes now wandered like a choir that had lost its leader. Nell lifted the lid, laid out her tuning hammer and felt, and coaxed each string back into line while the first guests drifted in. She finished by playing a short, simple tune to test the keys, with the calm of someone who knew exactly what had been wrong.

In the doorway stood a tall young man with sawdust on his sleeves, who had come in to escape the noise outside and stayed to listen. His name was Sam Adeyemi, the son of the boatbuilder at the far end of the lake, and he had never before watched anyone tune a piano. He hummed the tune a little off the key, and seemed to find it more interesting than the festival itself.

On the steps outside, they shared a bag of plums and discovered that both of them were about to leave. In September Sam would sail to Rotterdam to train as a ship's engineer, while Nell had been offered a place with a famous piano firm in the city. It was strange, she thought, to feel so sorry about losing someone she had known for only an hour.

At the water's edge they each wrote a wish on a paper lantern, shielding the words from one another with a curved hand. When they set the little boats of light upon the lake, the current carried them out side by side, and neither could look away. Nell found herself wondering what Sam had written and whether she would ever dare to ask.

Sitting at the end of the old Green Jetty with their feet above the dark water, Sam proposed a promise that sounded half like a joke and half like a plan. Wherever life took them, and whatever it did to them, they would meet on this spot every July at dusk. Nell shook his hand solemnly, though her heart was beating much too fast for a joke.

They talked until the sky above the lake turned the colour of pearl, and then there was nothing left to do but say goodbye. Nell climbed onto the first bus of the morning, pressed her forehead to the window and watched Sam grow smaller in the road until a bend took him away. She did not yet know that she would count the days until the next July.

At Marlowe & Sons, the great piano makers of the city, Nell spent her days among half-built instruments and her evenings in a rented room above a bakery. Letters arrived from Rotterdam every few weeks, filled with hurried drawings of engines, gears and the cranes of the harbour. She read each one twice, then put it away in a shoebox as though it were something fragile.

When July returned, Nell rode the slow train back to Linden Quay with her stomach full of nervous butterflies and a lantern wrapped carefully in her bag. Sam was already waiting at the end of the Green Jetty, browner and broader than she remembered, grinning as though no time had passed at all. They walked the whole way around the lake that evening, talking so fast that they kept finishing each other's sentences.

Near midnight Sam borrowed his father's rowing boat and took Nell out beneath the stars, showing off a little with each long, easy stroke. Halfway across he laughed so hard at one of her jokes that the whole boat rolled over and tipped them both into the warm black water. They surfaced spluttering and helpless with laughter, and Nell thought that she had never been so happy in her life.

Wrapped in dry blankets on the jetty, Nell felt the words rise in her throat and gather there, ready to be said. Sam, however, had begun to talk about his first posting on a cargo ship, his eyes bright with plans for the sea, and she could not bear to dim them. So she smiled, nodded and swallowed the words, telling herself that there was plenty of time.

Before her train left, Sam pressed a small brass bolt into her palm, a piece of ship's metal that he had threaded on a loop of string. It was a silly present, he admitted, but it had come from the first engine he had ever repaired, and he wanted her to have it. Nell hung it around her neck and wore it beneath her collar for years.

In her third year with the firm, Nell was chosen to care for the pianos at the Marlowe Concert Hall, a promotion she had hardly dared to hope for. There she met Dominic Reyes, a gentle, sensible dentist who adored music and played it with more enthusiasm than skill. He listened to her talk about hammers and strings with real wonder, and she liked him for it.

On the third Lantern Night, Nell reached the Green Jetty well before sunset, her lantern in her hands and her best dress on. The sky darkened, the music began in the hall, and the lights bobbed out across the water, yet there was no sign of Sam. She told herself that trains were often late, though by ten o'clock even she could no longer believe it.

Just before midnight a figure came stumbling along the shore, dusty and gasping, with a heavy bag banging against his back. His ship had been held up in port, Sam explained between breaths, and he had run the last three miles from the station rather than miss the evening altogether. Nell, who had meant to be furious, found that her anger melted the instant she saw his face.

They sat side by side on the jetty and watched the last of the lanterns gutter out one by one across the water. Neither spoke for a long while, and the silence between them felt neither empty nor awkward, but crowded with everything they were not saying. When the sky began to pale, Sam gave a small, rueful laugh, as if he too had been thinking the same thing.

In the spring a letter arrived in which Sam mentioned, with careful casualness, that he had met a woman named Corinne, a navigator who worked on his ship. Nell read the paragraph three times, folded the page into a small square and told the empty room that she was delighted for him. The room, which had known her for years and had heard every one of her small lies, did not believe it.

On the fourth Lantern Night, Sam came along the Green Jetty with a woman at his side, tall and cheerful, with dark curls tied back from her face. He introduced her as Corinne, and Nell shook her hand with a smile so bright and so practised that it almost hurt. Nobody standing on the jetty that evening could possibly have guessed what that smile had really cost her.

The worst of it was that Corinne was thoroughly likeable, with a quick laugh and a way of asking questions that made people feel interesting. Nell searched for some fault to hold against her and found nothing, which only made the evening harder to bear. Before the lanterns were lit she invented an early train and slipped away through the crowd.

On the long night bus back to the city, Nell turned the little brass bolt over and over between her fingers until the metal grew warm. Waiting for a man who was happy with someone else, she decided, was a poor way to spend a life, and it was time to look at who was actually in front of her. By the time the bus reached the terminal, she had made up her mind to accept Dominic's invitation to dinner.

For the next year, Nell and Dominic filled their weekends with concerts, long dinners and slow walks beside the river. He was steady, generous and entirely without drama, and he never once asked her to be anyone other than herself. If there was a small, quiet room in her heart that he never entered, she told herself that every heart has such a room.

Dominic had a conference that weekend, so Nell went to the fifth Lantern Night by herself and half wished she had stayed away. Sam was already on the jetty, thinner and quieter than before, and he told her without bitterness that he and Corinne had decided to go their separate ways. Nell murmured that she was sorry, and was ashamed to find that she was not entirely sure it was true.

Sam explained that he had accepted a place on a freighter bound for Asia, a voyage of nearly a year that would take him far beyond the reach of any post office. He did not know whether he could keep their promise the following July, and he would not ask her to wait for him. Nell nodded as though she understood, while the lake lay still and dark in front of them.

That winter, old Mr Brandt died, the patient tuner who had first shown Nell how to listen to a piano and had never doubted her. In his will he left her his tools, worn smooth by fifty years of use, and the small shop on Harbour Lane in Linden Quay. She stood at the back of the little church, holding the key, and felt the past reach out and take her by the hand.

Nell left the shop on Harbour Lane locked, though she visited it twice that spring and stood in the dusty silence among its covered pianos. Her job, her friends and Dominic were all in the city, and it seemed reckless to abandon a secure life for a dream she could scarcely describe. Still, the key stayed on her ring, and she could not bring herself to put the shop up for sale.

Knowing perfectly well that Sam was somewhere in the Indian Ocean, Nell went to the Green Jetty all the same and sat there until the final lantern had burned out. It was a foolish thing to do, and she did it with her eyes open, for the promise had been made to the jetty as much as to him. Around her, the festival went cheerfully on, with music and laughter and children, as if nothing in the world were missing.

Three weeks later a postcard arrived with a foreign stamp, a view of a crowded harbour and a message in Sam's cramped handwriting. On Lantern Night, he wrote, he had stood alone on the deck in the dark and pictured the whole lake covered in lights, and he had kept the promise in the only way he could. Nell read it standing in the hallway, and then she read it again sitting on the stairs.

In the autumn, Dominic took her to their favourite restaurant, fidgeted through the first course and then pushed a small velvet box across the tablecloth. His face was open and hopeful, without a shadow of doubt, and the ring inside caught the candlelight and held it. Nell understood, with a cold clear feeling, that she was about to disappoint the kindest man she knew.

She asked Dominic for a little time, and with typical grace he said that she could have as much as she needed. Nell walked home through the empty streets for hours, asking herself, honestly for the first time, what she wanted and where she wanted to be. Each time she tried to picture a future, it kept arriving at a shop on Harbour Lane and a lake full of lights.

On a bench beside the river, Nell told Dominic the truth as gently as she could, and her voice shook before she had finished. He was silent for a while, and then he took her hand and said that he had always known part of her was listening for a different piano. It was the most generous sentence anyone had ever spoken to her, and it made her cry harder.

On the seventh Lantern Night, Nell came to the Green Jetty feeling lighter than she had for years, carrying two lanterns instead of one. She had rehearsed what she would say, but the minutes ticked by, the music faded in the hall, and the shore stayed empty. At midnight, when the last lanterns had floated away and the crowd had gone home, she knew at last that nobody was coming.

Before she left, Nell tore a page from her notebook, wrote two words on it and folded it into a tight square. She wedged it under a loose stone beside the bench, in the hope that Sam might one day look there, though she knew how slender the hope was. The note said only I came, and she did not sign it, because she was sure that he would know who had written it.

On the train back to the city, Nell gazed at the passing fields and concluded that the promise had been nothing more than a game for two nineteen-year-olds. She felt foolish and exposed, like someone who had gone on knocking at a door long after the house had been sold. By the time the towers came into view she had resolved never to go back.

When the second Saturday of July came round again, Nell stayed in the city and buried herself in the preparations for an enormous summer festival. She tuned eleven pianos in four days, declined two invitations and informed everyone who asked that she did not mind in the least. It was a performance, and she gave it so well that she almost convinced herself.

Sam was home for good now, because his father had fallen ill the previous July, on the very day he had hoped to reach the jetty, and the boatyard had needed him ever since. On the second Saturday of this July he sat alone on the Green Jetty, noticed a loose stone beside the bench, and found beneath it a paper softened by a year of rain. Two words were written on it, in a hand he knew at once: I came.

The next morning Sam met Nell's younger sister Pip at the market, and she was in no mood to be polite, having watched Nell return to the city so miserably the year before. Only when he had explained everything about his father, and the hospital, and the note, did her face soften enough to give him the news he wanted. Nell, she said, was still tuning pianos at the Marlowe Concert Hall, and she did not come home as often as she used to.

That night Sam wrote Nell a long letter, and by the fourth page every sentence sounded either desperate or false. He tore it into small pieces, threw them into the stove and reached for a railway timetable instead, because some things have to be said to a person's face. He chose a Saturday in September, when the summer orders at the boatyard would be finished, and marked it with a thick pencil line.

In September, with the summer orders delivered, Sam took the early train to the city and walked into the empty Marlowe Concert Hall as if entering a church. On the great stage a woman was bent over the open lid of a grand piano, testing one note again and again, and he knew the set of her shoulders before she turned. He stood quite still at the back, afraid that the smallest sound would make her vanish.

Nell saw him, dropped her tuning hammer with a clang that echoed through the empty hall, and for a long moment neither of them moved. They walked beside the river for hours while he told her about his father's fall and the long nights at the hospital, and she told him about the loose stone and the two words. When they had finished, the sun was low, and something that had been tangled for years felt a little straighter.

On a stone bridge, as the street lamps flickered on one by one, Sam told her that he had loved her since the very first Lantern Night. He confessed that Corinne had known it long before he did, and that this was the real reason she had gone her own way. Nell gripped the cold stone of the parapet and found that she could not speak.

At last Nell admitted that she loved him too, and that this was exactly what frightened her, for she had spent years protecting herself from the chance of losing him. Sam listened without interrupting and then said, quietly, that he was a patient man, that boats had taught him patience, and that she should take as long as she needed. It was a promise, she realised, quite as binding as the one they had made at nineteen, and it did not need a handshake to seal it.

At midwinter Nell took the train to Linden Quay, walked through the snow to Harbour Lane and finally turned the key in the lock. The shop was thick with dust and bitterly cold, its old upright piano shrouded in a sheet like a patient asleep, yet she felt at once that she had come home. She stood in the middle of the floor and heard, in her mind, the whole place filled with music.

Back in the city, Nell carried her letter of resignation into Mr Marlowe's office and laid it on his desk with a hand that was almost steady. He read it twice, sighed with real regret and then rose to shake her hand, telling her that no one at the firm had ever listened to a piano so well. She left the building with a box of belongings and a feeling like a window opening.

In the spring Sam arrived with his father's old van and carried every one of Nell's boxes up the narrow stairs, refusing all offers of help. Pip stood on the pavement with her arms folded, grinning, and applauded each trip as though she were watching a sporting event. Nell stood in the doorway of her own shop, laughing so much that she forgot to be nervous.

Sam painted the sign himself, in deep blue with gold letters, and hung it above the door on a bracket he had forged in his father's yard. On the first morning of business, Nell stood beneath it with a cup of tea, reading the words Hartley Piano Tuning as though they belonged to somebody else. Her first customer, a farmer's wife with a cracked old upright, arrived before nine.

As the weeks passed they fell into the habit of seeing each other almost daily, over breakfast, along the shore and across the table in the shop. In the evenings Sam worked on a small wooden rowing boat in the corner of his father's yard, shaping each plank with such care that he would not tell her whom it was for. Nell pretended not to be curious, yet she found endless reasons to wander past the yard every second evening.

On the second Saturday of July, the festival committee asked Nell to tune the old upright in the hall once more, and she accepted with a glow of pride. When the work was finished she sat down at the keys, and almost without deciding to, she played the simple tune she had played on the very first night. It rang out through the empty hall as clearly and as sweetly as a bell.

As the last notes faded, she heard a voice from the doorway humming the same tune a little off the key, exactly as it had on that first night. Sam leaned against the frame with his arms crossed and a look of such open happiness that Nell burst out laughing. Without a word they walked together down the hill to the Green Jetty, where the lanterns were already being lit.

Tied to the end of the jetty bobbed a small new rowing boat, its planks pale and gleaming in the lantern light, with a single word painted on the bow. Lantern, it said, and Sam explained, with unusual shyness, that he had built it over the spring for two people to row on the lake, every July and every other month as well. Nell ran her hand along the smooth, cool wood of the gunwale, and for once in her life she could not think of a single word.

Each wrote a wish on a paper lantern, and this time they showed them to one another, and the two wishes were word for word the same. Sam kissed her on the Green Jetty with the whole lake glowing at their feet, while the two lanterns drifted out side by side, exactly as they had on the first night. They had promised at nineteen to meet every July, and now they would keep that promise for the rest of their lives, and every other day besides.
